source.title: The case for unlearning that removes information from LLM weights

record.file_problem: None; this is the full post and its comments, not the referenced paper’s full text.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports a fine-tuning-based evaluation of whether unlearning removed information, using a different measure from the unlearning methods themselves.
record.gate_note: The post summarizes the authors’ own experiments: after unlearning, fine-tune on one split of facts and measure accuracy on an independent held-out split. It reports results qualitatively, without model names or numerical accuracies. Cited jailbreak results and other papers’ results are not recorded as rows. The false-fact approach and other proposed removal strategies are not tested here.
record.test_reason: The authors' own retrain-on-T/evaluate-on-V (RTT) experiments test whether GD, RMU and RIA unlearning is undone by fine-tuning on a subset of the forgotten facts. This is a different method from the originals' benchmark, probing and jailbreak evaluations, aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that GD, RMU and RIA do not remove a significant fraction of pretrained facts from the weights; RTT recovers them, so these methods are closer to refusal training than to removal. After the bug fix, synthetic birthday facts fine-tuned in appeared genuinely removed, which they take as a warning against TOFU-style synthetic-fact evaluations.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes GD, RMU, and RIA unlearning, then evaluates retained information by retraining on a split of facts and measuring an independent split. This is a different evaluation recipe from the cited methods’ usual refusal, probing, or jailbreak-oriented evaluations.
record.method_sensitivity: The result differed between facts learned during pretraining and synthetic birthday facts learned by fine-tuning; the corrected birthday dataset did not show recovery. Recovery was also reported when facts were trained into one set of layers and gradient-ascent unlearning was applied to another.
record.problems: This post is a qualitative summary rather than the full experimental paper: it names no model checkpoints and supplies no numerical results, error estimates, or detailed control results. The authors also report a dataset bug that changed the random-birthdays finding; the corrected synthetic-fact result may not generalize to pretrained facts.
record.rows_left_out: No numerical rows were available in the post. The statement about failing to reproduce an external fine-tuning-robustness result is not recorded as a row because the method, attack conditions, and outcome details are not specified. Cited jailbreak and other-paper findings are excluded.

untested.parts: Whether targeted accuracy reached near chance and whether general ability was kept are not reported in the post.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data is not tested. The size of the relearning set is not stated.
Not tested; jailbreak recovery is only cited from other work.
There are no rows. The post only mentions failed reproduction of one fine-tuning-robust method and that RepNoise/TAR break under learning-rate or LoRA changes.

missing.what: Recovery persists even with very large unlearning coefficients that begin destroying the model
Authors' failed reproduction of a fine-tuning-robust unlearning method; a similar technique is broken by a better learning rate
missing.locator: Footnote 1 (Appendix C of paper); comment score 7

missing.what: Unlearning on plain-text facts rather than the MCQ format mostly doesn't change conclusions
missing.locator: 'mostly doesn't change the conclusions, as shown in Figure 4'

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog summary of arXiv:2410.08827, with no numbers or model names. r4 is a withdrawn buggy result and r6 is a method-validation control; both are unlinked. For r1–r3 and r5, a single state is shared across A and B. It is read as the presence of recovery, which is the opposite of what A predicts.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not report whether targeted accuracy was brought near chance or whether general ability was preserved. It does report whether retraining recovers held-out knowledge.
The reported retraining uses a subset of independent facts; unrelated or loosely related examples are not tested. The size of the retraining set is not stated.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis showing access-blocking rather than deletion is reported.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context-information prompting test is reported.

The post mentions an external fine-tuning-robustness claim and says its results were not reproduced, but provides no identifiable method, attack conditions, or results that test resistance to the attacks in this claim.

relation.reason: The post reports the authors' own RTT results (summarizing 2410.08827), plus the corrected random-birthdays rerun, on whether unlearning removes facts.

tranche.reason: The authors' own retrain-on-T/evaluate-on-V (RTT) evaluation is a different method from the originals' benchmark, probing and jailbreak evaluations. It addresses the same question: whether unlearned knowledge is still in the weights.

source_check.notes: The post summarizes 2410.08827 and gives no per-method or per-model numbers. r1-r3 are qualitative and the models are unnamed. Row states describe recovery (the phenomenon): for A they read inversely, as the rows' verdict fixes say. The corrected-birthdays comment says no recovery after unlearning and names no RMU exception (the paper's r19 shows one). The old flawed dataset did show recovery, and layer-split stress tests still recover.

statements.correction: On the corrected random-birthdays dataset (synthetic facts fine-tuned in before unlearning), RTT recovers no information after unlearning. The author says this kind of evaluation may overestimate unlearning reliability (n=1 dataset). In the same post, RTT does recover on all three pretraining-learned datasets: Years, MMLU and WMDP-deduped (r1-r3; no technique comes close to halving held-out accuracy). Unlearning methods and models are not stated for r5.
statements.problem: Cites r5 as a fine-tuning attack that fails, but leaves out key context. r5 is a single synthetic dataset fine-tuned in, which the author says may overestimate unlearning reliability. The conditions also list other recovering settings in the same studies but omit this post's recovery on Years, MMLU and WMDP-deduped (r1-r3). 'One model per setting' does not apply: the post names no models.
